title: Nehemiah 9:26–38
context: The prayer recounts a repeated cycle: Israel rebels, kills the prophets, and is handed to enemies; they cry out, and God in his manifold mercies sends saviors (compare Judges 2:16–18); then they turn to evil again. God testified against them by his Spirit through the prophets (compare Zechariah 7:12), yet they would not listen, and he gave them into the hands of the peoples, but in his mercy he did not make a full end of them. The people confess that God is just in all that has come on them, describe themselves as servants in their own land under foreign kings, and declare that they will make a sure covenant in writing, sealed by their leaders. Verse 38 in English Bibles, including the WEB, is numbered 10:1 in the Hebrew text, so the Hebrew chapter 10 begins one verse earlier. Arminian and Reformed readers commonly read the passage as shared ground about confessing God’s justice, trusting his mercy, and renewing commitment to his law.

verses.text: “Nevertheless they were disobedient and rebelled against you, cast your law behind their back, killed your prophets that testified against them to turn them again to you, and they committed awful blasphemies.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Israel rebelling, casting the law behind their backs, and killing the prophets. Rejection of God’s word is deliberate.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the confession as honest acknowledgment of persistent sin (compare 2 Chronicles 36:16). Both traditions commonly read the verse as a sober account of covenant unfaithfulness.

verses.text: Therefore you delivered them into the hand of their adversaries, who distressed them. In the time of their trouble, when they cried to you, you heard from heaven; and according to your manifold mercies you gave them saviors who saved them out of the hands of their adversaries.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see God giving the people over to enemies, then hearing their cry and sending saviors. Discipline is followed by mercy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the pattern of the judges, where God’s mercy repeatedly rescues his people (compare Judges 2:16–18). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as praise for God’s compassion.

verses.text: But after they had rest, they did evil again before you; therefore you left them in the hands of their enemies, so that they had the dominion over them; yet when they returned and cried to you, you heard from heaven; and many times you delivered them according to your mercies,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the cycle of rest, sin, discipline, and deliverance repeating many times. God’s patience is remarkable.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s repeated mercy as grounded in his covenant faithfulness (compare Psalm 78:38). Both traditions commonly read the verse as shared ground about God’s patient grace.

verses.text: and testified against them, that you might bring them again to your law. Yet they were arrogant, and didn’t listen to your commandments, but sinned against your ordinances (which if a man does, he shall live in them), turned their backs, stiffened their neck, and would not hear.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see God testifying against the people to bring them back to the law, which if a man does, he shall live in them. They see a sincere call to return.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same words as recalling the covenant promise of Leviticus 18:5, which Paul later cites (compare Romans 10:5). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse here as confession of Israel’s failure to keep that law.

verses.text: Yet many years you put up with them, and testified against them by your Spirit through your prophets. Yet they would not listen. Therefore you gave them into the hand of the peoples of the lands.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see God bearing with the people for many years and testifying by his Spirit through the prophets, yet they would not listen. They commonly see this as grace genuinely resisted.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the prophets’ message as the Spirit’s outward call, which hardened hearts refused (compare Zechariah 7:12; Acts 7:51). Both traditions commonly agree that the refusal was the people’s own and that God was patient.

verses.text: “Nevertheless in your manifold mercies you didn’t make a full end of them, nor forsake them; for you are a gracious and merciful God.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see God, in his manifold mercies, not making a full end of the people. Mercy limits judgment and leaves room for hope.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s preservation as rooted in his gracious and merciful character (compare Lamentations 3:22). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as hope in the midst of judgment.

verses.text: Now therefore, our God, the great, the mighty, and the awesome God, who keeps covenant and loving kindness, don’t let all the travail seem little before you that has come on us, on our kings, on our princes, on our priests, on our prophets, on our fathers, and on all your people, since the time of the kings of Assyria to this day.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the people appealing to the great, mighty, and awesome God who keeps covenant and loving kindness. They ask God to see their suffering.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the appeal as grounded in God’s covenant faithfulness (compare Daniel 9:4). Both traditions commonly read the verse as a model of honest petition.

verses.text: However you are just in all that has come on us; for you have dealt truly, but we have done wickedly.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the confession that God is just in all that has come on them. The people accept responsibility without excuse.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the acknowledgment of God’s justice as essential to true repentance (compare Daniel 9:7; 1 John 1:9). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as shared ground about honest confession.

verses.text: Also our kings, our princes, our priests, and our fathers have not kept your law, nor listened to your commandments and your testimonies with which you testified against them.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see kings, princes, priests, and fathers failing to keep God’s law. Failure reached every level of leadership.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the confession as acknowledging the corporate nature of sin. Both traditions commonly read the verse as humble recognition of the people’s history.

verses.text: For they have not served you in their kingdom, and in your great goodness that you gave them, and in the large and rich land which you gave before them. They didn’t turn from their wicked works.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the people failing to serve God even in his great goodness and the rich land. Blessing did not lead to faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as showing how prosperity can harden hearts (compare Romans 2:4). Readers in both traditions commonly read it as a warning against ingratitude.

verses.text: “Behold, we are servants today, and as for the land that you gave to our fathers to eat its fruit and its good, behold, we are servants in it.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the people describing themselves as servants in the land given to their fathers. They feel the weight of their situation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the lament as honest recognition of the consequences of sin (compare Ezra 9:9). Both traditions commonly read the verse with compassion for the people’s distress.

verses.text: It yields much increase to the kings whom you have set over us because of our sins. Also they have power over our bodies and over our livestock, at their pleasure, and we are in great distress.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the land’s increase going to foreign kings because of the people’s sins, leaving them in great distress. They name their suffering honestly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the confession as accepting God’s discipline while appealing for his mercy. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a sincere lament.

verses.text: Yet for all this, we make a sure covenant, and write it; and our princes, our Levites, and our priests, seal it.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the people making a sure covenant in writing, sealed by their leaders. Repentance leads to renewed commitment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the covenant as a fitting response to God’s mercy (compare Nehemiah 10:29). Both traditions commonly read the written pledge as gratitude expressed in concrete obedience.
